x.ASV: Cast thy bread upon the waters; for thou shalt find it after many days.
x.Darby: Cast thy bread upon the waters; for thou shalt find it after many days.
x.KJV: Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days.
x.YLT: Send forth thy bread on the face of the waters, For in the multitude of the days thou dost find it.

nt: שַׁלַּ֥ח לַחְמְ⁠ךָ֖ עַל פְּנֵ֣י הַ⁠מָּ֑יִם כִּֽי בְ⁠רֹ֥ב הַ⁠יָּמִ֖ים תִּמְצָאֶֽ⁠נּוּ

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if a person’s goods or efforts were **bread** thrown **on the face of the waters**, by which he means that they are given away in some sense. This could refer to: (1) being generous to others, which will bring a reward later, as in the UST, or (2) being willing to risk making an investment in something that should bring a profit at a future time. Alternate translation: [make investments now, because they will bring profit to you later]

x.ASV: Give a portion to seven, yea, even unto eight; for thou knowest not what evil shall be upon the earth.
x.Darby: Give a portion to seven, and also to eight; for thou knowest not what evil shall be upon the earth.
x.KJV: Give a portion to seven, and also to eight; for thou knowest not what evil shall be upon the earth.
x.YLT: Give a portion to seven, and even to eight, For thou knowest not what evil is on the earth.

nt: Qoheleth is using **to seven and even to eight** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to many.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to many people]
כִּ֚י לֹ֣א תֵדַ֔ע מַה־יִּהְיֶ֥ה רָעָ֖ה עַל־הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ

The implication is that these seven or eight people will help you when you are in need because you helped them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for you do not know what will be a misfortune on the earth, and when it happens, they will help you]

x.ASV: If the clouds be full of rain, they empty themselves upon the earth; and if a tree fall toward the south, or toward the north, in the place where the tree falleth, there shall it be.
x.Darby: If the clouds be full of rain, they empty themselves upon the earth; and if a tree fall toward the south, or toward the north, in the place where the tree falleth, there it shall be.
x.KJV: If the clouds be full of rain, they empty themselves upon the earth: and if the tree fall toward the south, or toward the north, in the place where the tree falleth, there it shall be.
x.YLT: If the thick clouds are full of rain, On the earth they empty themselves; And if a tree doth fall in the south or to the north, The place where the tree falleth, there it is.

nt: The expression **are filled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the clouds are full of rain]

Qoheleth is referring to all of the places where a tree might fall by naming two major components, **the south** and **the north**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in one direction or another]

x.ASV: He that observeth the wind shall not sow; and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap.
x.Darby: He that observeth the wind will not sow; and he that regardeth the clouds will not reap.
x.KJV: He that observeth the wind shall not sow; and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap.
x.YLT: Whoso is observing the wind soweth not, And whoso is looking on the thick clouds reapeth not.

nt: שֹׁמֵ֥ר ר֖וּחַ לֹ֣א יִזְרָ֑ע וְ⁠רֹאֶ֥ה בֶ⁠עָבִ֖ים לֹ֥א יִקְצֽוֹר

The implication is that a person who waits for perfect weather before he works will never get his work done. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [One who waits for the wind to be perfect will never sow his seed, and one who waits for the clouds to be perfect will never harvest his crops]

x.ASV: As thou knowest not what is the way of the wind, nor how the bones do grow in the womb of her that is with child; even so thou knowest not the work of God who doeth all.
x.Darby: As thou knowest not what is the way of the spirit, how the bones [grow] in the womb of her that is with child, even so thou knowest not the work ofGod who maketh all.
x.KJV: As thou knowest not what is the way of the spirit, nor how the bones do grow in the womb of her that is with child: even so thou knowest not the works of God who maketh all.
x.YLT: As thou knowest not what is the way of the spirit, How--bones in the womb of the full one, So thou knowest not the work of God who maketh the whole.

nt: The implication is that **the way of the wind** is something that people cannot understand. This could mean: (1) how the wind moves, where it comes from, and where it goes; or (2) how the breath of life enters the body of an unborn child, since the word translated **wind** can also mean “spirit” or “breath.” You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [is the path of the wind, where it comes from and where it goes]

Qoheleth is using **the bones** to represent the whole body of the unborn baby. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as the parts of the baby’s body]

Qoheleth is using **the full woman** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the pregnant woman.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the woman who is pregnant]

x.ASV: In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thy hand; for thou knowest not which shall prosper, whether this or that, or whether they both shall be alike good.
x.Darby: In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thy hand; for thou knowest not which shall prosper, whether this or that, or whether they both shall be alike good.
x.KJV: In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand: for thou knowest not whether shall prosper, either this or that, or whether they both shall be alike good.
x.YLT: In the morning sow thy seed, And at even withdraw not thy hand, For thou knowest not which is right, this or that, Or whether both of them alike are good.

nt: Qoheleth is referring to all of the day by naming two major components, **In the morning** and **in the evening**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [From morning until evening, sow your seed, and]
Here, **hand** represents “work.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [do not stop working]

The first **this one** refers to the seed sown in the morning, while the second **this one** refers to the seed sown in the evening. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the morning seed or the evening seed]

x.ASV: Truly the light is sweet, and a pleasant thing it is for the eyes to behold the sun.
x.Darby: Now the light is sweet, and pleasant is it to the eyes to see the sun;
x.KJV: Truly the light is sweet, and a pleasant thing it is for the eyes to behold the sun:
x.YLT: Sweet also is the light, And good for the eyes to see the sun.

nt: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if **light**, which represents being alive, were something that tastes **sweet**. It means that being alive is pleasant. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And being alive is pleasant]

Qoheleth is using **it is good for the eyes to see the sun** as a common expression of the culture to mean “it is good to be alive.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it is good to be living]

x.ASV: Yea, if a man live many years, let him rejoice in them all; but let him remember the days of darkness, for they shall be many. All that cometh is vanity.
x.Darby: but if a man live many years, [and] rejoice in them all, yet let him remember the days of darkness; for they shall be many: all that cometh is vanity.
x.KJV: But if a man live many years, and rejoice in them all; yet let him remember the days of darkness; for they shall be many. All that cometh is vanity.
x.YLT: But, if man liveth many years, In all of them let him rejoice, And remember the days of darkness, For they are many! all that is coming is vanity.

nt: If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. The word **For** introduces a further explanation of the previous statement, not a reason for it. Alternate translation: [Indeed, if]

Qoheleth is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a person]

Qoheleth is saying what he wants any person who lives many years to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [he should rejoice. But he should remember]

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if a time of death or trouble were **darkness**. This could mean: (1) the time after a person dies, when he will no longer see the light of the sun; or (2) times of trouble and sorrow during a person’s life. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the days when he will be dead]

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if everything that will happen were **vapor**. It means that everything that happens is temporary and does not last, like breath or mist that quickly disappears. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Everything that is coming is temporary and quickly passes away]

t: and/ let it make good/ you

x.ASV: Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth, and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth, and walk in the ways of thy heart, and in the sight of thine eyes; but know thou, that for all these things God will bring thee into judgment.
x.Darby: Rejoice, young man, in thy youth; and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth, and walk in the ways of thy heart, and in the sight of thine eyes; but know that for all these [things]God will bring thee into judgment.
x.KJV: Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth; and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth, and walk in the ways of thine heart, and in the sight of thine eyes: but know thou, that for all these things God will bring thee into judgment.
x.YLT: Rejoice, O young man, in thy childhood, And let thy heart gladden thee in days of thy youth, And walk in the ways of thy heart, And in the sight of thine eyes, And know thou that for all these, Doth God bring thee into judgment.

nt: Here the masculine term **young man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [young person]

Qoheleth is saying what he wants the young man’s **heart** to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [and I want your heart to make you glad]

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the way a person lives were walking on a path. He speaks of doing what a person desires as walking **in the ways of your heart** and of doing what a person sees and likes as walking **in the sight of your eyes**. It means that the young man should live by doing what he wants and what he sees that he likes. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And live by doing what you desire and what you see that you like]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **judgment**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [will bring you before him and judge you]

x.ASV: Therefore remove sorrow from thy heart, and put away evil from thy flesh; for youth and the dawn of life are vanity.
x.Darby: Then remove discontent from thy heart, and put away evil from thy flesh; for childhood and youth are vanity.
x.KJV: Therefore remove sorrow from thy heart, and put away evil from thy flesh: for childhood and youth are vanity.
x.YLT: And turn aside anger from thy heart, And cause evil to pass from thy flesh, For the childhood and the age are vanity!

nt: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if **anger** and **misfortune** were objects that a person could take away from his **heart** and his **flesh**. It means that the young man should not let himself stay angry or let troubles affect him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And do not stay angry, and do not let troubles affect your body]
Here, **dark hair** represents “the prime of life.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the prime of life]
